rotina.title: Daily routine · 1 to 1.5 hours, no calendar
rotina.intro:
The routine has **4 blocks**. The first two are the **core**: they keep your Japanese alive. The other two are **flexible**: add them when the day allows. Do them in whatever order fits your day; what matters is coming back tomorrow.
• The **course lesson** stays the same until you complete its checklist — that may take 2, 3 or 5 sessions, and that is fine.
• Review (SRS) comes first because it gives the most per minute.

blocks.name: Review (SRS)
blocks.what: Do all of today's reviews in the ヅオリンゴー app (🌊 All: vocabulary, grammar, kana and kanji together).
blocks.tools: App → 🌊 All · still on kana? the Kana Trail

blocks.name: Course lesson
blocks.what: Move forward in your current lesson following block 2 (the lesson plan): one or two parts per session, always out loud, notebook open.

blocks.name: Active practice
blocks.what: The lesson's homework (block 7), 🔬 Anatomy → Build from the end, or 3 sentences of your own in the app's Journal.

blocks.name: Immersion
blocks.what: Wagotabi, one of the lesson's videos, or something at your level from the Resources tab — for fun, understanding whatever you can.

rotina.minimum: On busy days, do only the Review (🌊 All) and write 1 sentence in the Journal — about 15 minutes. That still counts, and it is what stops forgetting.

cycle.title: The cycle of one lesson (usually 3 sessions)
cycle.body:
**Session 1 · understand:** blocks 1–4 (goals, vocabulary, grammar with examples out loud and 🔬) plus the video in block 6 and the matching **Sakubi** lesson (also in block 6) as a second explanation.
**Session 2 · lock it in:** the homework in your notebook (block 7), checking the answer key item by item, plus the Workbook pages.
**Session 3 · use it:** home practice (block 8: Wagotabi, the app, shadowing, recording yourself) and the checklist (block 10).
• If a checklist item does not click, add one more session just to review that point — that is the normal pace of real learning, not falling behind.
• When you finish a whole Genki lesson, do the app's Practice L# for that lesson before moving on.

week.title: A sample week (adapt freely)
week.body:
• **Mon–Fri:** the full routine (or the minimum day when needed).
• **Saturday:** lesson + a long Wagotabi or video session (30–40 min).
• **Sunday:** review + light immersion only (active rest).
• Mark the days in the grid above; whenever you like, click "New week" and start the grid over — there is no calendar to keep up with.

sections.title: How the course works
sections.body:
There are **102 lessons** in 6 parts: Unit 0 (kana and sounds), Genki I (N5), Genki II (N4), the N3 Bridge, review Milestones and the Travel Track (in parallel).
• Every lesson has the same **10 blocks**: goals, plan, prerequisites and vocabulary, grammar, how to study, videos and reading, notebook homework with answer key, home practice, culture, and a mastery checklist.
• A lesson is **mastered** when every checklist item is ticked. There are no dates: the **Continue** button always takes you to the next lesson you have not mastered.
• All content is original and follows the Genki order; the book remains your main reading — the course tells you **what** to read, **how** to study and **how** to practice.

sections.title: The milestone map
sections.body:
• **Unit 0:** read hiragana and katakana, greetings and numbers.
• **Milestone 1** (after Lesson 4): introduce yourself, talk about your routine, what exists and where, and the past.
• **Milestone 2** (after Lesson 8): describe, request, allow and forbid; short forms and casual speech.
• **Milestone 3 · N5** (after Lesson 12): all of Genki I — the N5 foundation.
• **Milestones 4 and 5 · N4:** all of Genki II — the basics of keigo, passive/causative, conditionals.
• **Milestone 6 · N3 Bridge:** everyday intermediate grammar and strategies for native material.
• **Travel Track:** start after lesson 06-4 and do it in parallel.

sections.title: How to study each lesson
sections.body:
• **Read from the end.** In Japanese the predicate (verb, adjective or です) comes last and rules the sentence. Find it first, then ask: who? what? where? when? — each particle answers one of those questions. The 🔬 on every example shows this in color.
• **Out loud, always.** Read the examples aloud and tap 🔊 to compare.
• **Notebook by hand.** Homework is for writing, not just thinking; mistakes in the notebook are what make it stick.
• **Check the key item by item.** Do not reveal everything at once: mark the mistake, read the 💡 reason, redo it the next day.
• **✍️ and 📱.** Tick ✍️ when you understand a point and 📱 when you practice it outside the course (Wagotabi, the app, conversation). Use 📝 for your notes.

sections.title: What each tool is for
sections.body:
• **This course:** tells you what to study now and how — the map.
• **Genki I/II (the book):** explanations, dialogues and textbook exercises — the main reading for each lesson.
• **Genki Workbook:** exercises; every lesson says which pages to do (check them with the official Answer Key).
• **The ヅオリンゴー app:** spaced repetition (🌊 All), Practice L#, Drills (conjugation, numbers, particles, 🔬 Anatomy), Kana, Kanji, Journal and Immersion — and this course inside the 🏫 Course tab.
• **Wagotabi:** immersion as a game, ordered by JLPT; every lesson suggests what to hunt for in its dialogues.
• **genki-companion:** the checklist of the 77 Genki I points (you can import its marks under Progress).
• **kana-flow / kana-speed-trainer:** kana fluency and speed while reading is still slow.

sections.title: Your two best free companions: Sakubi and the DJT guide
sections.body:
• **Sakubi** (sakubi.neocities.org) is a free grammar guide in plain English. Block 6 of every lesson links the matching Sakubi lesson: read it after the grammar block as a second explanation — a different angle often makes a point click.
• The **DJT guide** (djtguide.neocities.org/guide) explains the method many self-learners follow: learn kana, read one grammar guide from start to finish, build vocabulary with spaced repetition, then read real Japanese while collecting new words. This course is your grammar guide; the ヅオリンゴー app is your spaced repetition; Wagotabi and the Resources tab are your reading and listening.
• Its **Resource Guide** lists tools by skill (kana, kanji, vocabulary, grammar, practice, Anki, dictionaries, typing). Use the links in the Resources tab and skip anything that asks you to download copyrighted books.
• When you finish Genki I, re-read the DJT section "Now what do I do to actually learn Japanese?": it is the plan for moving from textbook to native material.

sections.title: Golden rules
sections.body:
• **Consistency beats intensity.** 20 minutes every day beats 3 hours on Sunday.
• **The minimum day exists.** On bad days: review + 1 sentence. That is not failing.
• **Mastery, not the calendar.** There is no "behind". If a lesson needs more sessions, it needs more sessions.
• **Going back is not going backwards.** Revisiting a mastered lesson is studying.
• **Your sentence > the book's sentence.** Whenever you learn a point, make a true sentence about your own life.
• **Understand the block, not the word.** When you get lost in a sentence, find the predicate and tag the blocks.

sections.title: When you get stuck
sections.body:
• **Lost in the sentence:** 🔬 Anatomy → Build from the end (in the app) and the 🔬 on the lesson examples.
• **Forgetting vocabulary:** make sure your reviews (🌊 All) are up to date; fewer new words per day, more review.
• **Conjugation won't come out:** app → Drills → Conjugation, 5 minutes a day until it is automatic.
• **Can't understand the audio:** shadow the examples (🔊): listen, repeat along, repeat again.
• **No motivation:** do a Travel Track lesson, play Wagotabi, or pick something from Resources — a change of angle is still studying.

sections.title: After the course
sections.body:
• After the N3 Bridge, the natural next step is an intermediate textbook (Tobira or Quartet) plus **reading and listening to native material** every day (NHK Easy, manga with furigana, podcasts, shows with Japanese subtitles).
• The **JLPT is optional**: a way to validate a milestone, not the goal. If you want to take it, check dates and test sites on the official Japan Foundation website for your country.
• N2 and N1 are mostly about **volume**: thousands of hours of reading and listening, steady kanji, and spaced review. The routine of this course still works — just with more native material.
